1.pericope_label: And in the seventh month, on the first day of the month, ye shall have an holy convocation; ye shall do no servile work: it is a day of blowing the trumpets unto you. And ye shall offer a burnt offering for a sweet savour unto the LORD; one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs of the first year without blemish: And their meat offering shall be of flour mingled with oil, three tenth deals for a bullock, and two tenth deals for a ram, And one tenth deal for one lamb, throughout the seven lambs:

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin cover the month and the arithmetic. Gill identifies the seventh month as Tisri, as the Targum of Jonathan renders it, answering to part of our September and October, and calls it a month famous for days to be religiously observed, having more of them in it than any other month in the year. On the meat offering he explains that it went along with the creatures offered for a burnt offering, the quantity of flour and oil being the same for a bullock, a ram and each lamb as in the offerings at the new moons, the feast of unleavened bread and the day of firstfruits, and that a kid of the goats was also offered for a sin offering at this time, as in those seasons and for the same purpose, to make atonement for the sins of their holy things. Calvin observes that the festivals are not here treated of but only the sacrifices by which their solemnisation was to be graced, and that in the beginning of the seventh month was the memorial, as it was called, of the blowing of trumpets. Because it was a minor festival, he says, Moses only commands one bullock to be killed; but the number was increased on other grounds, for on the first of every month two bullocks were sacrificed, so that this day had three larger victims while the number of the others was doubled, two rams and fourteen lambs. God thus consecrated this day doubly to himself, so that one celebration diminished nothing of the other, else he might have seemed to have abrogated what he had once commanded: the memorial of trumpets was not an abolition of the new moon, but they kept both ordinances at the same time.

Henry accounts for the month and draws the lessons. There were more sacred solemnities in the seventh month than in any other month of the year, not only because it had been the first month till the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, which, falling in the month Abib, occasioned that to be thenceforth made the beginning of the months in all ecclesiastical computations, but because it still continued the first month in the civil reckonings of the jubilees and years of release, and also because it was the time of vacation between harvest and seedtime, when they had most leisure to attend the sanctuary — which intimates that, though God will dispense with sacrifices in consideration of works of necessity and mercy, the more leisure we have from the pressing occasions of this life the more time we should spend in the immediate service of God. He describes the day of blowing the trumpets as a preparative for the two great solemnities of holy mourning on the day of atonement and of holy joy in the feast of tabernacles, and says the intention of divine institutions is well answered when one religious service helps to fit us for another and all for heaven. Since the blowing of the trumpets was appointed in Leviticus without any mention there of these sacrifices, Henry infers that those who would know the mind of God in the scripture must compare one part of the scripture with another and put together those parts that have reference to the same thing, the latter discoveries of divine light explaining what was dark and supplying what was defective in the former. He notes the care taken that these sacrifices should not supersede the daily oblation or that of the new moon, and turns it into a rule: we must not seek occasions to abate our zeal in God's service, nor be glad of an excuse to omit a good duty, but rather rejoice in an opportunity of doing more than ordinary in religion; if we perform family worship we must not think that this will excuse us from our secret devotions.

Clarke supplies the calendar and the comparative note. This was the beginning of their civil year, he says, and was a time of great festivity, ushered in by the blowing of trumpets; it answers to a part of our September. In imitation of the Jews different nations began their new year with sacrifices and festivity: the ancient Egyptians did so, and the Persians still celebrate their nawi rooz, or new year's day, which they hold on the vernal equinox, the first day of the year being generally a time of festivity in all civilized nations. On this day, he records, the Israelites offered one young bullock, one ram, seven lambs, and a kid, for a sin offering, besides minchahs or meat offerings.

debates: Why the seventh month carries so many solemnities. Henry gives three reasons — that it had been the first month before the exodus, that it remained first in the civil reckoning of jubilees and years of release, and that it fell in the vacation between harvest and seedtime; Gill records only that it is famous for having more such days than any other month; Clarke locates the density in the opening of the civil year and in a festivity common to the nations.

Why only one bullock is commanded here. Calvin explains it as proper to a minor festival, but argues the day was not therefore poorer, since the two bullocks of the new moon stood alongside it and made three in all; Clarke simply totals what was brought without raising the question.

What the day was for. Henry makes it preparatory to the mourning of the atonement and the joy of tabernacles; Calvin declines to treat the festival at all, holding that the chapter is about the sacrifices that graced the festivals rather than the festivals themselves; Gill treats it as one of the month's many observed days.

What the kid was for. Gill specifies atonement for the sins of their holy things, on the analogy of the new moons, unleavened bread and firstfruits; Clarke names it a sin offering without assigning it an object.
outliers: Clarke alone looks outside Israel, setting the new year's sacrifices beside the practice of the ancient Egyptians and the Persian nawi rooz kept at the vernal equinox.
Henry alone reads the agricultural calendar as a reason for the placing of the solemnities, arguing that God set them where the people had least other work to do.
themes: a day of blowing the trumpets
a burnt offering for a sweet savour
one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs
three tenth deals for a bullock
one tenth deal for one lamb

6.pericope_label: Beside the burnt offering of the month, and his meat offering, and the daily burnt offering, and his meat offering, and their drink offerings, according unto their manner, for a sweet savour, a sacrifice made by fire unto the LORD. And ye shall have on the tenth day of this seventh month an holy convocation; and ye shall afflict your souls: ye shall not do any work therein: But ye shall offer a burnt offering unto the LORD for a sweet savour; one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs of the first year; they shall be unto you without blemish: And their meat offering shall be of flour mingled with oil, three tenth deals to a bullock, and two tenth deals to one ram, A several tenth deal for one lamb, throughout the seven lambs: One kid of the goats for a sin offering; beside the sin offering of atonement, and the continual burnt offering, and the meat offering of it, and their drink offerings.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin divide the span. Gill explains that the bullock, ram and seven lambs were offered on this day besides the two bullocks, one ram and seven lambs which were offered on it on account of its being the first day of the month, and besides the meat offering that went along with them, these not being omitted on account of the additional sacrifices. On the tenth day he again gives the month as Tisri, following the Targum of Jonathan. He takes the burnt offering of the tenth day to be the same as was ordered to be offered on the first day, but reports that Aben Ezra is of opinion that the ram here is different; and he notes that the meat offering was of the same quantity of flour and oil, for a bullock, a ram and a lamb, as for the meat offering on the first day of the month. On the kid of the goats for a sin offering he observes that, as it was different from that which was offered for the service of the day, so it was offered after it, as is observed by the Jewish writers, that the goat which was offered without, though of the Musaphim or additions, could not go before the service of the day. Calvin identifies the tenth day as the day of Atonement: although they never came into God's presence without supplication for pardon, they then in a special manner confessed their sins, because a fast was appointed in token of their guilt, for it is written in Leviticus that whatsoever soul shall not be afflicted in that same day shall be cut off from among his people. As to the sacrifices, one bullock only is required and the rest is as before, except that an exception is added which was omitted in the former cases, for another propitiation is appointed besides the goat, to accord with the fact of their affliction; the acknowledgment of guilt, Calvin adds, would have been a dreadful torment to their consciences without the hope of reconciliation.

Ellicott handles the wording and the legislation. On the burnt offering of the month he prefers of the new moon, referring to the previous chapter where the burnt offering of the beginning of the month is described. On the tenth day of this seventh month he notes that the law respecting the observance of the great Day of Atonement is contained in Leviticus 16 and Leviticus 23:26-32, and that the sacrifices prescribed here, which are the same as those prescribed for the first day of the seventh month, were to be offered in addition to the sin offerings of atonement prescribed in Leviticus 16 and to the daily burnt offerings. On the command to afflict the soul he refers again to Leviticus, and judges that this affliction or humiliation appears to have included in it fasting, comparing the reference in Acts 27:9, although the word which denotes fasting is not employed, nor is there any express injunction respecting fasting in the Pentateuch.

Clarke refers the reader to his notes on Leviticus and adds nothing here. Wesley glosses two phrases. Of the month, he says, means belonging to every new moon. To afflict your souls means yourselves, by fasting and abstinence from all delightful things, and by compunction for your sins, and the judgments of God, either deserved by you or inflicted upon you.

debates: What the command to afflict the soul required. Wesley takes it directly of fasting and abstinence from all delightful things, with compunction for sin and for God's judgments; Calvin treats the fast as appointed and as the token of guilt, citing the penalty of being cut off; Ellicott agrees that fasting was probably included but points out that the word for fasting is not used here and that the Pentateuch nowhere expressly enjoins it.

Why a further sin offering was needed on a day already given to atonement. Calvin holds that a second propitiation was added to match the people's affliction, since the acknowledgment of guilt without hope of reconciliation would have tormented the conscience; Ellicott states the relation mechanically, that these sacrifices stood in addition to the atonement sin offerings and the daily burnt offerings; Gill answers from the order of service, that the additional goat could not precede the goat of the day itself.

What the burnt offering of the month is. Ellicott would render it of the new moon and refers to the previous chapter's description; Wesley glosses it as belonging to every new moon; Gill uses it to insist that the additional sacrifices displaced neither the monthly nor the daily offering.
Whether the ram of the tenth day is the ram of the first. Gill takes the whole offering to be the same as that of the first day, but records Aben Ezra's opinion that the ram here is a different one.
outliers: Ellicott alone refuses to read a command to fast out of the passage, observing that the term for fasting is absent and that no express injunction to fast appears anywhere in the Pentateuch.
Gill alone approaches the additional goat through the rabbinic rules of precedence, holding that a sacrifice of the Musaphim could not be offered before the service proper to the day.

the tenth day of this seventh month
ye shall not do any work
one kid of the goats for a sin offering
beside the sin offering of atonement

12.pericope_label: And on the fifteenth day of the seventh month ye shall have an holy convocation; ye shall do no servile work, and ye shall keep a feast unto the LORD seven days: And ye shall offer a burnt offering, a sacrifice made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD; thirteen young bullocks, two rams, and fourteen lambs of the first year; they shall be without blemish:

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin open the feast. Gill dates it to the fifteenth day of the same month Tisri, which was the seventh from Nisan or Abib, though it was formerly the first month of the year, and notes that the burnt offering which follows was that of the first of the seven days. Calvin holds that among their festivals this last was the chief, in which they dwelt in tabernacles for seven days; for whereas in the Passover they commemorated the night in which they came forth free from the plagues of Egypt, by dwelling in tabernacles they embraced the whole forty years in which their fathers in the desert experienced the constant and consummate bounty of God. That solemn convention also availed for another present purpose, of thanksgiving to God for the ingathering of the harvest, which is why they offered sacrifices every day and in greater number: on the first day thirteen bullocks, two rams and fourteen lambs; on the second twelve bullocks; on the third eleven; on the fourth ten; on the fifth nine; on the sixth eight; on the seventh seven; and on the eighth one. Nor is it carelessly, he adds, that Moses expends so many words on the recital, but that nothing might be done except at God's command, lest it should be disagreeable or onerous to be at such great expense, which they would gladly have avoided; that they might cheerfully obey, he diligently inculcates what victims God would have daily offered. But why the distribution was so unequal, Calvin confesses, is not clear to him, and it is better to confess his ignorance than by too subtle speculations to vanish into mere smoke. He allows that Scott's conjecture is not without force, that the decrease of the number of bullocks until on the last and great day only one was offered is the most observable circumstance in this law, and that the reason is not evident unless it be intimated that the Mosaic institution would gradually wax old and at length vanish away when the promised Messiah came. As a specimen of the ancient opinions he subjoins from De Lyra that the Hebrews say the offerings were made for other nations, and therefore seventy calves were offered altogether, according to the number of the seventy nations divided into seventy languages, the daily decrease designating that the dominion of the Gentiles was to be diminished and terminated under King Messiah, to whom all nations are to be subdued; this notion, he says, is neither curious nor to be rejected. What Calvin affirms for himself is that by daily diminishing the number they came at last on the seventh day to the number seven, which is the symbol of perfection, the eighth being superadded merely as a conclusion; and that in the continual sacrifice as well as in these extraordinary ones they should hold fast to what God prescribes, so that nothing should be altered according to man's fancy.

Henry draws a series of observations from the ordinance. Their days of rejoicing were to be days of sacrifices, and a disposition to be cheerful does us no harm, nor is it any bad symptom, when it is so far from unfitting us for the duties of God's immediate service that it encourages and enlarges our hearts in them. All the days of their dwelling in booths they must offer sacrifices; while we are here in a tabernacle-state it is our interest as well as duty constantly to keep up communion with God, nor will the unsettledness of our outward condition excuse us in neglecting the duties of God's worship. The sacrifices for each of the seven days, though differing in nothing but the number of the bullocks, are severally and particularly appointed, which is no vain repetition, for God would teach them to be very exact in those observances and to keep an eye of faith fixed upon the institution in every day's work; it likewise intimates that the repetition of the same services, if performed with an upright heart and with a continued fire of pious and devout affection, is no weariness to God, and therefore we ought not to snuff at it. The number of bullocks, which were the most costly part of the sacrifice, decreased every day: thirteen on the first, twelve on the second, eleven on the third, so that on the seventh they offered seven; and the last day, though it was the great day of the feast and celebrated with a holy convocation, they were to offer but one bullock, and whereas on all the other days they offered two rams and fourteen lambs, on this they offered but one ram and seven lambs. Such was the will of the Law-maker, and that is reason enough for the law. Some suggest, Henry reports, that God herein considered the infirmity of the flesh, which is apt to grudge the charge and expense of religion, so that it is ordered to grow less and less lest they should complain as if God had made them to serve with an offering; or it is hereby intimated that the legal dispensation should wax old and vanish away at last, and the multitude of their sacrifices should end in one great sacrifice infinitely more worthy than all of them. It was on the last day of the feast, after all these sacrifices had been ordered, that our Lord Jesus stood and cried to those who still thirsted after righteousness, being sensible of the insufficiency of these sacrifices to justify them, to come unto him and drink. Henry adds that the meat offerings and drink offerings attended all the sacrifices according to their number, after the manner, since be there ever so much flesh it is no feast without bread and drink, and these must never be omitted at God's altar, which was his table; that every day a sin offering was presented, since our burnt offerings of praise cannot be accepted of God unless we have an interest in the great sacrifice of propitiation which Christ offered; and that even when all these were offered the continual burnt offering must not be omitted either morning or evening, since no extraordinary services should jostle out our stated devotions.

Clarke and Wesley take opposite scales. Clarke records that on this day there was to be a solemn assembly, and for seven days sacrifices were to be offered: on the first day thirteen young bullocks, two rams and fourteen lambs, and on each succeeding day one bullock less, till on the seventh day there were only seven, making in all seventy. What an expensive service, he exclaims, and how should we magnify God for being delivered from it — yet these were all the taxes they had to pay. At the public charge there were annually offered to God, independently of trespass offerings and voluntary vows, fifteen goats, twenty-one kids, seventy-two rams, one hundred and thirty-two bullocks, and eleven hundred and one lambs; but how little is all this, he adds, compared with the lambs slain every year at the passover, which amounted in one year to 255,600 slain in the temple itself — the answer that Cestius, the Roman general, received when he asked the priests how many persons had come to Jerusalem at their annual festivals, the priests numbering the people by the lambs that had been slain and saying twenty-five myriads, five thousand and six hundred. Wesley confines himself to the phrase: keeping a feast seven days meant not abstaining so long from all servile work, but offering extraordinary sacrifices each day. This was the Feast of Tabernacles, and all the days of their dwelling in booths they must offer sacrifices; while we are in these tabernacles it is our interest as well as duty to keep up our communion with God, nor will the unsettledness of our outward condition excuse our neglect of God's worship.

Ellicott states the scale and the reason for it. A larger number of burnt offerings was appointed for this feast than for any other festival: seventy oxen in all were to be offered on the seven days, the number being diminished by one daily, thirteen on the first day, twelve on the second, eleven on the third, and in like manner until the seventh day, on which seven oxen, the perfect number, were to be offered. In addition to the oxen, two rams and fourteen lambs were to be offered daily as burnt offerings, and a he-goat as a sin offering, in addition to the daily burnt offering, with the appointed meal offerings and drink offerings accompanying all the burnt offerings. The large number of the sacrifices offered at this time, Ellicott judges, may be accounted for from the consideration that at this feast the people not only expressed their gratitude for the Divine presence and protection, but also for the rich fruits of the harvest which had been recently ingathered.

debates: Why the number of bullocks falls each day. Henry answers first that the will of the Law-maker is reason enough, then reports the suggestion that God spared a flesh apt to grudge the expense of religion, then proposes that it figures the legal dispensation waxing old and ending in one great sacrifice; Calvin declines to decide, confessing the reason is not clear to him, though he grants Scott's version of the same messianic reading and records De Lyra's report that the Hebrews took the seventy calves for the seventy nations and the decrease for the waning dominion of the Gentiles; what Calvin will affirm is only that the series arrives at seven, the symbol of perfection, a reading Ellicott reaches independently in calling seven the perfect number.

Why this feast carried more sacrifices than any other. Calvin traces it to what was commemorated, the whole forty years of desert provision rather than a single night, together with harvest thanksgiving; Ellicott gives the divine presence and the recent ingathering; Henry makes the joy of the occasion itself the reason for the sacrifices; Clarke registers only the cost.

What the length of the recital is for. Calvin holds that Moses is not careless but is securing that nothing be done except at God's command, and that the expense not be resented; Henry, that the several appointment of each day is no vain repetition but a lesson in exactness, and that repeated service offered with an upright heart is no weariness to God.

What keeping the feast seven days consisted in. Wesley denies that it means abstaining from servile work throughout, and makes it the daily extraordinary sacrifices; Henry treats the whole period of dwelling in booths as the time of offering; Calvin makes the dwelling itself the commemoration.
outliers: Clarke alone counts the national cost, totalling the annual public charge and then setting even that beside the number of passover lambs the priests reported to Cestius.
Calvin alone refuses to explain the descending number and says so openly, preferring a confessed ignorance to what he calls vanishing into mere smoke by too subtle speculation.
themes: the fifteenth day of the seventh month
a feast unto the LORD seven days

34.pericope_label: And on the seventh day seven bullocks, two rams, and fourteen lambs of the first year without blemish: On the eighth day ye shall have a solemn assembly: ye shall do no servile work therein: But ye shall offer a burnt offering, a sacrifice made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD: one bullock, one ram, seven lambs of the first year without blemish:

schools.summary: Gill treats the eighth day as an appendage. It fell on the day after the seven days of the feast of tabernacles were ended, for this was not properly a part of that feast but a sort of appendage to it. On the offering he explains that the burnt offering was the same that was offered on the first and tenth days of this month, and that the meat and drink offerings for each of the creatures were the same, as has often been expressed; and that on this day a goat for a sin offering was also offered, besides the daily sacrifice and what went along with that.

Clarke rates the day higher than the others do. Among the Jews, he reports, this was esteemed the chief or high day of the feast, though fewer sacrifices were offered on it than on the others; the people seem to have finished the solemnity with a greater measure of spiritual devotion. He adds that it was on this day of the feast that our blessed Lord called the Jews from the letter to the spirit of the law, proposing himself as the sole fountain whence they could derive the streams of salvation, and refers the reader to his notes on Leviticus for the feast as a whole.

Ellicott works from the word and its uses. He would render the phrase closing feast day rather than solemn assembly. The word azereth, which is here and in the parallel passage in Leviticus rendered solemn assembly, is used in Deuteronomy of the seventh or closing day of the Feast of the Passover, and is used in Jeremiah and in Amos in a more general manner: in the former of an assembly or confederacy of false dealers, and in the latter it appears to include solemn festivals generally, without limitation to the last day of their duration. The primary notion, Ellicott concludes, appears to be that of restraint, that is, from the performance of servile work. He notes further that the sacrifices of the eighth day were the same as those which were appointed for the first day of the seventh month, the Feast of Trumpets, and also for the tenth day, the Day of Atonement.

debates: What the eighth day is. Gill makes it no part of the feast but an appendage following its close; Clarke reports that the Jews esteemed it the chief or high day of the feast; Ellicott declines both labels and renders it the closing feast day.

What azereth means. Ellicott argues from its use in Deuteronomy of the closing day of the Passover, and from its looser uses in Jeremiah of a confederacy of false dealers and in Amos of festivals generally, that the primary notion is restraint from servile work rather than assembly.

How much weight the smaller offering carries. Ellicott and Gill both note that the day's sacrifices simply repeat those of the first and tenth days of the month; Clarke observes that fewer were offered here than on the preceding days and yet holds this the day the people kept most devoutly.
outliers: Ellicott alone reaches his rendering by tracing the word outside the Pentateuch, and lets uses in the prophets overturn the sense the English version gives it.
Clarke alone treats the reduction in sacrifice as no reduction in the day's standing, reading a greater measure of spiritual devotion into the smaller offering.
themes: seven bullocks, two rams, and fourteen lambs
one bullock, one ram, seven lambs
of the first year without blemish

39.pericope_label: These things ye shall do unto the LORD in your set feasts, beside your vows, and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your meat offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings. And Moses told the children of Israel according to all that the LORD commanded Moses.

schools.summary: Gill corrects the rendering and then reads the last verse for its substance. On the phrase translated in your set feasts he prefers or rather in the times set and appointed to you, as the Jewish writers interpret it, and notes that Jarchi interprets it of a fixed time, which seems better to him; since these were not all feast days on which the above sacrifices were to be offered, for one of them was a fast, even the day of atonement. On the closing verse he says that Moses told the children of Israel all these things, repeating the several laws unto them concerning the above sacrifices, with the additions unto them and explanations of them, according to all that the Lord commanded Moses, being a faithful servant to the Lord in all his house and in all things appertaining to it.

Ellicott and Keil take the two verses differently. Ellicott would render the first better as These sacrifices shall ye offer unto the Lord at your set seasons, and explains the clause that follows: the sacrifices prescribed in this chapter were appointed to be offered independently of all the burnt offerings, meal offerings, drink offerings and peace offerings which were made in performance of special vows or as freewill offerings, referring to the regulations in Leviticus 22:18-21 and Numbers 15:1-13. On the last verse he records that in the Hebrew Bible it forms the beginning of the thirtieth chapter. Keil places the same verse the other way, holding that it forms the conclusion of the list of sacrifices in chapters 28 and 29.

debates: How the phrase rendered set feasts should be read. Gill rejects feasts outright, following the Jewish writers and Jarchi in taking it of times set and appointed, on the ground that the day of atonement was a fast and not a feast; Ellicott reaches the same correction by rendering it set seasons.

What the chapter's sacrifices stand beside. Ellicott holds that they were appointed independently of the burnt, meal, drink and peace offerings brought in performance of special vows or as freewill offerings, so that the public charge left the private offering untouched.

Where the closing verse belongs. Keil takes it as the conclusion of the list of sacrifices running through chapters 28 and 29; Ellicott records that the Hebrew Bible makes the same verse the opening of chapter 30; Gill, who comments on neither division, reads it simply as the record of Moses discharging what he was commanded.
outliers: Ellicott alone notices that the chapter division itself is disputed, so that the verse closing the chapter in the English opens a chapter in the Hebrew Bible.
Gill alone rests his correction on a named rabbinic authority, preferring Jarchi's fixed time to the English feasts because one of the days in view was a fast.
themes: these things ye shall do unto the LORD
Moses told the children of Israel
